_: FILM 4 -- The Monkey and the Wedge (panch-more).
THE PRIMITIVE IS `troop`: a crowd that is CAST, not scenery. docs/02 §5.7 puts crowds in
the plate because they never recur -- true of a village looking up, false of these
monkeys, who come down off the wall, try the saw and pull the wedge. A crowd of one cell
fails one way and fails completely: identical animals, evenly spaced, facing the same way,
breathing in step. So the rig places them AND varies them, from a seeded generator so the
render stays byte-identical, and film.js asserts no two neighbours share both size and
facing and that nobody stands inside anybody.
`n` is the whole crowd; there is no per-instance field, so the variation cannot be quietly
undone by hand-placing one of them.
THE LOG IS FILM-LEVEL, and that is not a second primitive -- it is the `rock` lesson at a
quarter of the size, and it is here because the first draft of this shot list got the log
wrong twice while it was still prose. The moral shot asked for a log held open by its
wedge AND a loose wedge lying beside it, which is two wedges in a story about one. And the
two cells came back at different proportions, so placing them by height -- as every other
sprite in the pipeline is placed -- would have made the log 24% LONGER at the exact cut
where it snaps shut. rig.log now owns its x, its ground line and its length; a shot may
write only:
"log": {}                                     as the carpenters left it
"log": { "shut": true }                       after he heaves the wedge out
"log": { "astride": { ... } }                 with somebody sitting on it
"log": { "shut": true, "wedge": true }        the wedge now on the ground
A loose wedge while the log is still open is refused at build time. `astride` puts his
bottom edge ON the log's top edge, so he cannot hover over the gap or sink into it.
CAST COST: zero. The monkey was drawn for story two.
